```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
load( "../results/aggregated_simulation_results.RData" )
require(tidyverse)

scenarios = expand.grid( 
  K = c(10), 
  J.bar = c(20,50),
  p.bar = c(0.5),
  ATE.district = 0.2, 
  sd.district = 0.1,
  ICC.district = 0.2,
  variable.J = c(T,F),
  variable.p = c(T,F),
  
  # cluster-level params
  n.bar = c(50), 
  sd.school = c(0.1), 
  ICC.school = 0.2,
  variable.n = c(T,F),
  
  # size and correlation params
  size.impact.cor.district = c(0,0.75),
  size.impact.cor.school = c(0,1),
  proptx.impact.cor.district = c(0,0.75))

vary_colsJ <- c("J.bar", "variable.J", "variable.n", "variable.p", 
               "size.impact.cor.district", "size.impact.cor.school",
               "proptx.impact.cor.district")
vary_cols <- c("variable.J", "variable.n", "variable.p", 
               "size.impact.cor.district", "size.impact.cor.school",
               "proptx.impact.cor.district")

key_methods <- c("LR w/ CRSE", "LR (agg)", "MLM")
```

## Picking representative models

```{r}
cor_mat <- function(d, value, lab=F) {
  d %>% 
    select(ID, method, val={{value}}) %>% 
    pivot_wider(names_from=method, values_from=val) %>% 
    select(-ID) %>% 
    cor() %>% 
    ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot(type="lower", 
                           lab = lab,
                           show.diag=T)
}

names(sruns)
cor_mat(sruns, bias.f.stu)
cor_mat(sruns, bias.f.dstu)
cor_mat(sruns, bias.f.sch)
cor_mat(sruns, bias.f.dsch)

cor_mat(sruns, RMSE.f.stu, lab=T)
```

```{r, include=F, eval=F}
complete_odyssey_results <- readRDS("~/R/clusterRCTsim/results/complete_odyssey_results.rds")
foo <- complete_odyssey_results$run[[1]]

foo <- foo %>% 
  select(subrun, method, ATE.hat, SE.hat)

foo %>%
  select(-SE.hat) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=method, values_from=ATE.hat) %>% 
  select(-subrun) %>% 
  cor() %>% 
  round(2)
```

Conclusions:

* LR with CRSE = LR (agg, wt) = DB_indiv (FE) $\approx$ DB_indiv (int)
* LR (agg) = DB_clust (int) = DB_clust (FE)

So just use LR with CRSE, LR (agg), and MLM

```{r}
sruns2 <- sruns %>% 
  filter(method %in% c("LR w/ CRSE", "LR (agg)", "MLM"))

cor_mat(sruns2, bias.f.stu, lab=T)
cor_mat(sruns2, bias.f.sch, lab=T)
```



## Breaking down simulations

Let's identify when models are biased for the non-district-weighted estimands.

```{r}
sruns2 %>%
  select(ID, method, bias.f.stu, bias.f.sch) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=abs(bias.f.stu), y=abs(bias.f.sch), label=ID)) +
  geom_text() +
  geom_abline() +
  facet_wrap(~method) 
```


Let's generate the two clumps.
Note that the IDs in the clumps are the same across methods.
Also note that J.bar doesn't affect things
```{r}
b_expected <- sruns2 %>% 
  filter(abs(bias.f.stu) > 0.02 & method == "LR (agg)") %>% 
  pull(ID)

sruns2 %>% 
  filter(method == "MLM", J.bar == 50) %>% 
  select(ID, all_of(vary_colsJ)) %>% 
  mutate(class = case_when(ID %in% b_expected ~ "biased_expected",
                           TRUE ~ "unbiased")) %>% 
  arrange(ID)
```

Conclusion: for usual estimands, correlating treatment effects with school sizes induces expected biases.


## Same as above, but for district stuff

Now for the district-weighted estimands.

```{r}
sruns2 %>%
  select(ID, method, bias.f.dstu, bias.f.dsch) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=abs(bias.f.dstu), y=abs(bias.f.dsch), label=ID)) +
  geom_text() +
  geom_abline() +
  facet_wrap(~method)
```

Weird! Now we get that the methods may be biased for neither, either, or both of the estimands!
Let's generate the four clumps.
Note that the clumps are the same for all of the methods.
Also, J.bar doesn't affect the clumps, so I'll just look at J.bar = 50.

```{r}
b_neither <- sruns %>% 
  filter(method == "LR (agg)", abs(bias.f.dstu) < 0.01, abs(bias.f.dsch) < 0.01) %>% 
  pull(ID)
b_both <- sruns %>% 
  filter(method == "LR (agg)", abs(bias.f.dstu) > 0.02, abs(bias.f.dsch) > 0.02) %>% 
  pull(ID)
b_weird <- sruns %>% 
  filter(method == "LR (agg)", abs(bias.f.dstu) < 0.01, abs(bias.f.dsch) > 0.02) %>% 
  pull(ID)
b_expected <- sruns %>% 
  filter(method == "LR (agg)", abs(bias.f.dstu) > 0.02, abs(bias.f.dsch) < 0.01) %>% 
  pull(ID)

sruns %>% 
  filter(method == "MLM", J.bar == 50) %>% 
  select(ID, all_of(vary_colsJ)) %>% 
  mutate(class = case_when(ID %in% b_neither ~ "unbiased",
                           ID %in% b_both ~ "biased_both",
                           ID %in% b_expected ~ "biased_expected",
                           ID %in% b_weird ~ "weird"))
```

Conclusions:
* Unbiased when: no size-impact correlations at school and district level
* Biased as expected when: size-impact correlation at school level but not at district level
* Biased for both when: size-impact correlation at district level but not at school level
* Weird when: size-impact correlation at both school and district level

Takeaways:
* Only thing that matters is size-impact correlations (i.e., proptx correlations, J.bar don't matter)


## Conclusions

Size-impact correlations matter.
We can facet by these size-impact correlations.

```{r}
sruns2 %>% 
  group_by(method, size.impact.cor.school, size.impact.cor.district) %>% 
  summarize(across(starts_with("bias"), ~mean(abs(.)))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("bias")) %>%
  mutate(finite = str_detect(name, ".f"),
         estimand = as.factor(str_extract(name, "([^.]+$)"))) %>% 
  mutate(estimand = factor(estimand, levels= c("stu", "dstu", "sch", "dsch"))) %>% 
  filter(finite) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=method, y=value, fill=estimand)) +
  geom_col(position="dodge") +
  facet_grid(size.impact.cor.school ~ size.impact.cor.district, labeller = "label_both")
```

For bias, we see the expected stories:
* no bias if no correlations
* bias for district-weighted estimands if only district correlations
* expected bias for non-district-weighted estimands if only school correlations
* chaos if both! expected bias for non-district-weighted estimands; for district-weighted estimands, backwards bias for LR (agg) and MLM, just much more bias than expected for LR w/ CRSE.




Uhhh... not clear that any of these are actually that far off?

## Checking: is MLM always targeting student-weighted?

MLM is pretty consistently worse at sch (which it's good at nonetheless), and better at stu (which it's bad at regardless)

```{r}
sruns %>% 
  filter(method %in% c("LR (agg)", "MLM"),
         size.impact.cor.district == 0,
         size.impact.cor.school == 1) %>% 
  select(ID, method, starts_with("bias")) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=abs(bias.f.stu), y=abs(bias.f.sch), color=method, label=ID)) +
  geom_text() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.012), xlim=c(0,0.055))
```

Could be worth checking scenarios that exacerbate this behavior?



## To do in simulation 2

More futzing around with the correlations!

### Correlation results

```{r}
load( "../results/aggregated_simulation_results2.RData" )
```

```{r}
sruns %>% 
  filter(method %in% key_methods) %>% 
  group_by(method, size.impact.cor.school, size.impact.cor.district) %>% 
  summarize(across(starts_with("bias"), ~mean(abs(.)))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("bias")) %>%
  mutate(finite = str_detect(name, ".f"),
         estimand = as.factor(str_extract(name, "([^.]+$)"))) %>% 
  mutate(estimand = factor(estimand, levels= c("stu", "dstu", "sch", "dsch"))) %>% 
  filter(finite) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=method, y=value, fill=estimand)) +
  geom_col(position="dodge") +
  facet_grid(size.impact.cor.school ~ size.impact.cor.district, labeller = "label_both")
```

Results:
* zero school-level correlation: all methods unbiased for non-district-weighted estimands. If district-level correlation is nonzero, all methods biased for district-weighted estimands.
* zero district-level correlation: if school-level correlation is nonzero, all methods biased as expected for student/school estimands.

Chaos reigns on the diagonals! LR (agg) and MLM are the same, but...
* Same sign correlation: MLM and LR (agg) biased for stu (expected) and dsch (why?), LR w/ CRSE biased for dstu (why?), sch (expected), dsch (expected but magnitude is huge)
* Different sign correlation: in reverse! LR w/ CRSE biased for sch (expected) and dstu (why?), other two biased for dsch (why?), stu (expected), dstu (expected but magnitude is huge)



REASON: we're just adding biases together!
Clearly the corners of the plot below are just sums of the sides

```{r}
sruns %>% 
  filter(method %in% key_methods) %>% 
  group_by(method, size.impact.cor.school, size.impact.cor.district) %>% 
  summarize(across(starts_with("bias"), mean)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("bias")) %>%
  mutate(finite = str_detect(name, ".f"),
         estimand = as.factor(str_extract(name, "([^.]+$)"))) %>% 
  mutate(estimand = factor(estimand, levels= c("stu", "dstu", "sch", "dsch"))) %>% 
  filter(finite) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=method, y=value, fill=estimand)) +
  geom_col(position="dodge") +
  facet_grid(size.impact.cor.school ~ size.impact.cor.district, labeller = "label_both")
```

```{r}
  mutate(finite = str_detect(name, ".f"),
         estimand = as.factor(str_extract(name, "([^.]+$)"))) %>% 
  mutate(estimand = factor(estimand, levels= c("stu", "dstu", "sch", "dsch"))) %>%

```

Might be some effect?
Hard to tell...

### Conclusion:

Results when both impact correlations are nonzero are confusing because they are the sum of the effects of changing each of the correlations!
Sometimes the effects magically cancel out and you're left with no bias!

So:

1. Correlating district impacts with district sizes leads to bias for district-weighted estimands
2. Correlating school impacts with school sizes leads to bias for non-target estimands (both district-weighted and non-district-weighted)

Also, sample size might matter?

## Final takeaways

1. We have three methods: LR with CRSE, MLM, LR (agg). 
The first two target student-weighted estimands, the last targets school-weighted estimands

2. Correlating district impacts with district sizes leads to bias for all district-weighted estimands, i.e., none of our methods are good at targeting the district-weighted estimands

3. Correlating school impacts with school sizes leads to bias for non-target estimands (both district-weighted and non-district-weighted)

4. Sample sizes don't strongly affect results. 
Often increasing data makes estimators significantly more biased for the estimands they're not trying to target.

5. Not sure how to get MLMs to more closely target a given estimand. MLMs just generally have more school-estimand bias, less student-estimand bias than LR (agg).

6. Changing ICCs doesn't really affect things either?
